items.title: Adjacency list vs. matrix: how the cost scales as the network grows
items.description: The flight network above has 6 cities and stays sparse — each city connects directly to only a few others. Drag the number of cities and the average number of direct routes per city to see how a matrix's V² cost pulls away from a list's V+E cost as the network grows. At the defaults (6 cities, ~2 routes each), this reproduces the scenario's own numbers: a 5-edge, 6-city network.
items.compute: const edges = Math.round((params.cityCount * params.avgRoutesPerCity) / 2); const listCells = params.cityCount + 2 * edges; const matrixCells = params.cityCount * params.cityCount; return { listCells, matrixCells };

items.title: Why the on-call system can't just check every service pair
items.description: The service dependency scenario above has 3 services in a tight triangle, but a real system has many more. Drag the total number of services and the average number of direct dependencies each one has to compare BFS's exploration cost (roughly one step per edge and node it actually walks) against brute-force checking every possible pair of services for a relationship. At the defaults (12 services, 3 dependencies each — a typical small microservice cluster), BFS is already far cheaper, and the gap only widens as the system grows.
items.compute: const edges = params.serviceCount * params.avgDependenciesPerService; const bfsSteps = params.serviceCount + edges; const bruteForceChecks = (params.serviceCount * (params.serviceCount - 1)) / 2; return { bfsSteps, bruteForceChecks };
